brief.idea: two teenagers who argue on the same train every morning realise they are both writing the same school play

premise.title: The Last Local
premise.logline: Aanya must get her scattered play pages back from Kabir before the train reaches Churchgate, or her play—and any chance with him—will be credited to the wrong name.
premise.theme: The person you argue with every morning may already know the ending you are trying to write.
premise.hook: A hanging strap becomes a tug-of-war between Aanya and Kabir; the train jerks, and identical pages spill from both bags—same title: The Last Local.
premise.stakes: If the scripts mix up, both are disqualified, Aanya loses the one story she meant, and Kabir's words reach the school in her voice.

spine: Once upon a time, Aanya and Kabir rode the same Mumbai local every morning and argued over the same window seat, the same hanging strap, the same air.
Every day, Aanya hid her school play in her book, Kabir hid his in his bag, and they traded insults from Andheri to Churchgate.
Until one day, a lurch of the train sends both manuscripts flying open, and each cover reads The Last Local.

Because of that, each accuses the other of copying, and they scramble to collect the scattered pages before Churchgate, reading each scene aloud until Aanya hears Kabir's ending—the one she could not write—and Kabir hears his own words in h
Until finally, the train pulls in, the teacher waits, and instead of one winner they hand in a single script with both names, their hands touching on the same strap as the doors open.
Ever since then, they still argue on the 8:17, but now they share the window seat, the strap, and the pen.

setup.what: Aanya folds the last page of her play into her book and rewrites dialogue in the margin, guarding the book on her lap.
If the play misses the gate, it's not mine anymore.
The route sign counts down to Churchgate, and a note tucked in Aanya's book reads: DRAMA SCRIPTS COLLECTED AT CHURCHGATE GATE.
Both Aanya's book and Kabir's bag hold scripts titled The Last Local, though neither notices.

beats.say: Aanya takes the page.
Aanya folds her last page into her book, beside the drama notice.
Aanya, that's my seat. Obviously.
Aanya gets up off the window seat.
Kabir taps the window twice and drops into the window seat.
Aanya takes the pencil from behind her ear and writes in the margin of her play, The Last Local.
Miss the gate at Churchgate and my play goes in under someone else's name.
Relax. Nobody's stealing the play behind your book.
You read it, Kabir.
I looked at the seat. The seat was empty.
Obviously it was empty. I was standing.
Kabir unzips his bag; his script, The Last Local, sits on top.
Same seat tomorrow. Same argument. Same time.
Obviously.
The lurch throws Kabir's bag down; Aanya's page slides out, and both read The Last Local.
You copied my title. Obviously.
Relax. It's obviously mine.
Obviously, the hero waits. Page nine.
I'd miss my stop for you'?
I did.
So did I.
Kabir takes the coach.
A jerk throws Kabir down the coach to the far end.
The same jerk slides Aanya into Kabir's old place.
First to Churchgate keeps the lot.
Aanya crouches as her folded last page skids under the seat.
Obviously you copied me. Give me my ending and keep the title.
Kabir shuts his bag and the zip jams on his final scenes.
Relax. My goat's been in this play since June.
Wait for me at the last local.
That's my line. Word for word.
Kabir goes over to the page.
Kabir takes up the folded page that slides back along the floor.
Not that one. Don't.
It's the good one. Don't change a word.
Aanya gets up and grips the hanging strap with both hands.
Kabir gets up; his hand lands on the strap over Aanya's.
Aanya laughs.
Aanya goes over to the script.
Aanya takes up Kabir's script as the train jerks.
Aanya looks at the Churchgate sign as the train slows.
Kabir gives Aanya his last pages.
She rides past her stop. All the way to the end of the line.
I couldn't write that. Nine drafts, and she always gets off.
Relax. Half of it's mine anyway.
Aanya crouches and pins the loose pages at the door.
Give me your ending. Both names, one script, before the door opens.
Kabir takes the spare pen out of the bag.
One b. I'm not losing my name to your spelling.
Kabir gives Aanya the pen.
Aanya signs both names at the top of the script as the doors rattle open.
Aanya steps out through the door with the script.
Aanya comes in.
Aanya held up.
Kabir taps the window twice.
That's not a doorbell, Kabir.
Kabir gives Aanya the pen.
No fight. No lecture. Are you ill?
Relax. I'm being nice. Don't tell anyone.
Aanya stands up out of the window seat as the train jerks.
Kabir drops into the window seat.
Aanya laughs.
Kabir stands up out of the window seat as the train jerks again.
Aanya drops back into the window seat.
Fight me for it. It's tradition.
Not today. Today I'm being nice too.
Aanya taps the window twice.
